summary: A Chrome extension condenses a page's CSS into a 10,000-token budget and asks a small local model (via Ollama) for additive CSS addressing 18 WCAG/cognitive-accessibility metrics. Six 7B-14B open models were tested on 10 violation-rich and 10 accessible live sites, scored manually by a single evaluator. Unverified edits improved 24 and regressed 20 of 100 trials, with no significant effects. The authors then built an audit-inject-verify loop (axe-core plus custom probes) on a 42-page seeded trilingual benchmark, validated only with stub generators, not models.

claims.claim: Unverified small-model CSS repair improves and regresses pages at similar rates.
claims.evidence: Table 3/§5.2: 24 improvements vs 20 regressions over 100 trials of five producing models; 56/100 trials no net change; t tests p .62-1.0, no sign test below .219; StarCoder2 produced no valid CSS in 20/20.

claims.claim: Verified repair loop detects 57/57 seeded violations with no false positives and rejects 126/126 harmful candidates.
claims.evidence: Table 5, real Chromium, but with ground-truth and adversarial stub generators, not any LLM; the guarantee covers only the auditor's own CSS-decidable checks.

claims.claim: Regression on automated checks is impossible by construction.
claims.evidence: Accept rule: violations must strictly decrease with no new violation type, else rollback. True by construction for the checked subset; regressions outside the auditor's checks are not covered.

patterns.note: Audit-inject-verify accept/rollback gate; validated as an instrument but not yet run with any model.
Human-triggered, reversible changes; human spot checks retained.

methodology.sample: Study 1: 6 models x 20 live sites = 120 planned trials, single manual scorer; Study 2: 42 seeded local pages (3 locales).
methodology.baselines: None beyond before/after; no larger-model or rule-based fixer comparison.
methodology.models: Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, DeepSeek-R1 8B, StarCoder2 7B, Gemma 3 12B, Code Llama 13B, Phi-4 14B (Ollama default quantization).
methodology.variance: One trial per model-site; sign and Fisher tests; sensitivity |d|≈1.0.

standards.peer_review: Accepted at ICMI 2026 companion proceedings (comment says ICME/ICMI, ACM).
standards.artifacts: Figshare replication package (extension, prompts, rubric, benchmark, harness, summary data); trial-level live-site records available on request only.
standards.preregistration: Directional hypotheses set at α=.05 a priori; no registry.

biases.detail: 10 sites per condition per model; single evaluator, no inter-rater reliability.
Verification instrument validated only on the authors' own seeded benchmark with stub generators.
The 'verified repair' headline characterises the checker, not repair by any model.

coi.affiliations: University of Southern Denmark (all five authors).

verdict_reason: Off-topic for this knowledge base: a user-side browser CSS-repair agent with small local models, not a software-engineering agent harness. The verified loop was never run with a model, and Study 1 is a small single-rater null result.
applicability: Does not transfer to backend Java services or harness design. The only generic lesson is to accept agent edits only when a deterministic checker shows strict improvement with no new violation types, and roll back otherwise; that is already the execution-verifier pattern. If the team's callers need accessibility checks for domain data, an axe-core gate in the front-end CI is the relevant takeaway, and it belongs to the front-end teams, not this harness.

conflicts_with.detail: Reports LLM (Kimi K2.5) accessibility fixes improving compliance in 80.2% of instances, versus near-parity improve/regress here with 7-14B local models. The gap likely reflects model scale and source-level vs user-side CSS repair.
